title: Senior's toolkit: joins you can trust
summary: Find the join paths, check the grain, write anti-joins that survive NULLs, and reconcile two systems.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: joins you can trust
steps.body: A join that runs is not a join that is right. Experienced people look up the foreign keys first, check that the "one" side really is one, and compare row counts before and after.

toolkit.what: Show a table's foreign keys, which tell you how tables join. In psql, `\d orders` lists them under "Foreign-key constraints" and "Referenced by".
flags: SQLite: the columns of t that point to other tables
psql: keys out of and into the table

toolkit.cmd: SELECT COUNT(*) before and after the join
toolkit.what: The fan-out check. If joining orders to payments turns 1,000 orders into 1,300 rows, some orders have several payments and every SUM over orders is now inflated.
flags: more rows means a one-to-many you did not plan for
sum the many side in a subquery or CTE, then join
toolkit.example:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id;

toolkit.cmd: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL
toolkit.what: The anti-join: rows with no match. `NOT EXISTS` says the same thing and is often clearer; both are safe with NULLs, unlike `NOT IN`.
flags: keep left rows whose match is missing
the same, written as a question
returns nothing if the subquery yields one NULL

toolkit.what: Reconcile two sources: rows only in A, only in B, and in both with different values (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite 3.39+).
flags: WHERE a.id IS NULL OR b.id IS NULL
OR a.amount IS DISTINCT FROM b.amount
toolkit.example:
SELECT COALESCE(l.id, b.id) AS id, l.amount AS ledger, b.amount AS bank
FROM ledger l
FULL JOIN bank b ON b.id = l.id
WHERE l.id IS NULL OR b.id IS NULL OR l.amount IS DISTINCT FROM b.amount;

toolkit.what: Join each row to a subquery that can use that row's columns: the clean way to get "the latest order per customer" (PostgreSQL `LATERAL`, SQL Server `CROSS APPLY` / `OUTER APPLY`).
flags: the top row per outer row
toolkit.example:
SELECT c.name, last.placed_at
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT placed_at FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 1
) last ON true;

toolkit.what: `o.id`, `c.id`: always say which table a column comes from once two tables are involved. It prevents "ambiguous column" errors and silent mistakes when someone adds a column with the same name later.
flags: qualify both sides of every condition

steps.prompt: After adding a join to `payments`, March revenue went from 84,200 to 109,460. Nothing else changed. What happened?
code: JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
options: Some orders have several payments (split or retried), so their total is counted once per payment; aggregate payments per order first, or use EXISTS
The join dropped orders without payments, which raised the total
The date filter must move into the ON clause
steps.explain: A one-to-many join repeats the "one" side. Dropping unmatched orders would lower the total, not raise it. Count rows before and after the join to catch this before anyone sees the report.

steps.prompt: This query should list customers who never ordered. It returns **zero rows**, although you know there are some. Why?
steps.code: SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
options: At least one `orders.customer_id` is NULL, and `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is never true; use `NOT EXISTS` or a LEFT JOIN anti-join
`NOT IN` only works with literal lists
steps.explain: `NOT IN` means `<> every value`, and `id <> NULL` is UNKNOWN, so no row passes. `NOT EXISTS` asks a yes/no question per customer and ignores NULLs.

steps.prompt: Two ways to list customers with no orders.
code: LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE __2__ (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
steps.explain: Test a column of the right table that can never be NULL in a real match, such as its primary key. A nullable column like `total` would also match orders whose total is NULL.

steps.prompt: Match each join to the job.
pairs: only orders that have a customer
every customer, with their orders if any
compare the ledger with the bank export

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before you trust a join, know the keys (read the foreign keys), know the grain (count before and after) and qualify every column. Write "has no match" as `NOT EXISTS`, never as `NOT IN` over a column that can be NULL.
